title: Onramp Lightning Playflows - Annotated Quickstart Notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight, actionable quickstart for an engineer integrating Redwood SDKs into a small sample app in under 20 minutes. Focus is on the minimum path that showcases: authentication, a single request flow (chat or generation), local stubbing for iterative dev, and basic telemetry hooks so the DX team can validate usage signals.

Audience:
- Product engineers evaluating Redwood for a feature spike
- Internal advocates who run quick demos for prospects
- New hires in partner companies doing self-serve integrations

Principles guiding this playflow:
- Minimal friction: get a running request in < 20 minutes.
- Observable by default: every sample wires basic telemetry (latency, token counts).
- Resilient for demos: include a deterministic local stub fallback.
- Small diff: examples are single-file or two-file setups to reduce cognitive overhead.

Quick architecture (1-paragraph):
Client app -> SDK wrapper (1 small helper) -> Redwood endpoint (hosted) or local stub (dev)
Telemetry sinks: console + lightweight metrics client (Prometheus/exporter example).

3-step lightning recipe (the one to memorize):
1) Credentials & environment: create API key (docs link), set REDWOOD_API_KEY in environment, install sdk-client (npm/pip).
   - npm: npm install @redwoodai/sdk
2) Minimal call: copy-paste the single-file sample below, run, confirm a valid response.
3) Swap in local-stub: flip a single ENV var (REDWOOD_LOCAL_STUB=true) and confirm the app returns the stubbed payload.

Single-file Node sample (annotated):
// Note: copy into quickstart/demo.js and run `node demo.js`
const Redwood = require('@redwoodai/sdk');
const client = new Redwood.Client({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
const useStub = process.env.REDWOOD_LOCAL_STUB === 'true';
async function run() {
  if (useStub) {
    // fast deterministic stub for offline demos
    console.log('Using local stub ->', { id: 'stub-1', output: 'Hello stub world' });
    return;
  }
  const res = await client.chat({ model: 'gpt-lite-1', messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Hello, world' }] });
  console.log('tokens:', res.token_usage, 'latency_ms:', res.latency_ms);
  console.log('response:', res.choices[0].message.content);
}
run().catch(e => console.error('demo error', e));

Local stub design notes:
- Keep stub deterministic and tiny (idempotent outputs).
- Return same envelope shape as hosted API (tokens, choices, meta) to avoid conditional logic in demos.
- Stub should be shipped as a tiny file in the repo: quickstart/stub.js.

Telemetry and what we want to capture during onboarding:
- request latency_ms (median and p95)
- token counts (prompt vs completion)
- success/failure (HTTP 2xx vs 4xx/5xx)
- environment: dev/demo vs CI vs prod (tag)
Implementation hints:
- For Node quickstarts, use console.log + a small metrics client wrapper that exposes a /metrics endpoint (Prometheus). Docker snippet included in full doc repo.
- For Python quickstarts, show both requests-based minimal example and an asynchronous aiohttp variant.

Common friction points & recovery steps (for advocates running demos):
- "Invalid API key" -> check env var name, confirm no extra whitespace; run `echo $REDWOOD_API_KEY | wc -c` to ensure length.
- Network allowed-listing -> remind to open outbound to api.redwood.ai:443 or use local stub.
- Slow response on first request (cold start) -> recommend running a warmup at start of demo (fire a tiny call right after process starts).

Prompts & Evaluation check (short):
- Include a tiny evaluation snippet in the quickstart that asserts the response contains expected tokens (used by advocates to verify demo health).
- Example: assert(res.choices[0].message.content.includes('Hello'))

Local development utilities (these are the small experimental bits we want in repo):
- quickstart/dev-proxy: lightweight proxy that rewrites requests to a local model or stub.
- quickstart/stub.js: returns a stable example response with metadata.
- quickstart/collect-telemetry.sh: launches the sample + a Prometheus exporter to capture basic metrics for a minute.

Checklist for the doc artifact we will publish:
- [ ] Single-file Node and Python samples
- [ ] Stub file included with matching envelope
- [ ] Troubleshooting FAQ (5 items)
- [ ] Telemetry minimal integration example
- [ ] One GIF or terminal recording showing the 3-step flow (for marketing/demo page)
- [ ] Short paragraph: "When to use the stub vs live"

Open questions (to resolve with eng/runtime & product):
- Should the quickstart default to the hosted endpoint or local stub on first clone? (tradeoff: friction vs false confidence)
- Which model should be the canonical example? (gpt-lite-1 vs text-curie-2 style) -> Product wants a low-cost, stable model for demos.
- Acceptable telemetry retention for quickstarts (we cannot send PII) -> security opinion needed.

Follow-ups and next steps (owners):
- Maya: draft the GIF and record terminal session. (ETA 2025-02-20)
- Jordan: small metrics wrapper + /metrics example (ETA 2025-02-14)
- Avery: finalize quickstart language and publish to SDK repo (ETA 2025-02-18)

Notes to self / scratches (keep informal):
- Consider a "first 60s" checklist pinned at top of README: env set, install, run, verify.
- Might add a one-click cloud token generator for marketing demos (needs security review).
- Keep language imperative and tiny — people scanning will copy/paste, not read long paragraphs.

References and links to internal tickets: JIRA-ENG-1423 (canonical quickstart), JIRA-DX-58 (telemetry wrapper), PR: github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-examples/pull/412

End.
